clue.text: Major defeat embarrassed winger, according to Spooner

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of the two words trade places

blocks.note: someone embarrassed goes red in the face
a winger is something with wings, here a black bird
swap the opening sounds BL and CR

explanation.surface: A sports report: the team's winger had an embarrassing game and the side lost heavily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' looks like a footballer on the flank, but here it is any creature with wings, a crow.
explanation.definitionFit: A crushing blow is a devastating setback, a heavy loss or reverse, which is what a major defeat amounts to.

clue.text: Bit hot in erected shelter

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
to put up a tent is to camp, so having erected shelter is having camped

explanation.surface: Someone bit into something hot while sitting in a tent they had pitched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit' reads as a noun (a small piece) but is the past tense of bite; 'erected shelter' is a verb phrase, CAMPED, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To champ is to munch or chew noisily, so champed is a past-tense synonym for bit, as a horse champs at its bit.

clue.text: Suspect wrong’uns after Golf gets trashed? It’s not confirmed

indicators.note: something trashed is thrown away, so that letter is discarded from the word list
something suspect is dodgy or unsound, so the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Shady characters are blamed after a golf course is vandalised, but nothing has been proved yet.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the G from WRONGUNS and rearrange the rest. A wrong'un is British slang for a crook.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement that is unsworn has not been made under oath, so it has not been formally confirmed or attested.

clue.text: Rider uses one husky, picked up wife with it

indicators.note: to pick something up is to hear it, so a word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a husky voice is a rough, hoarse one
W is the abbreviation for wife
to be with it is to be hip, fashionable

explanation.surface: A sled driver's husky dog is described alongside his wife, as if in a family snapshot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Husky' suggests a sled dog, but it is the adjective meaning hoarse. 'with it' together means fashionable, giving HIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A horsewhip is the crop or whip a horseman carries, so it is literally a thing a rider uses.

clue.text: Recalled right name of chap

indicators.note: something recalled is called back, so the word runs back the way it came

blocks.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: Someone remembered a man's correct name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right' is not R here but the legal right, a lien.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil is a common masculine first name, so it is an example of what a chap might be called.

clue.text: On vehicle, lout heading north is speedy type

indicators.note: in a down entry, going north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: RE means on or about, as in a memo
a car is a vehicle
a yob is a British word for a lout

explanation.surface: A hooligan perched on a car heads up the road at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string RE + CAR + YOB is reversed, not just the lout. A boy racer is British slang for a young man who drives a souped-up car too fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy racer is a young driver who loves going fast, so he is a speedy type of person.

clue.text: Dismissing exteriors, mock the grey paint

indicators.note: throwing away the outsides of each word leaves only what is inside them

blocks.note: the inside of the word
the inside of the word
the inside of the word

explanation.surface: Someone ignores the outside of a house and laughs at its dull grey paintwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Every one of the three words loses its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy yellow-brown pigment used to colour paint, so it names a kind of paint.

clue.text: Romeo’s written in orange-pink pen

indicators.note: words written in something are set down inside it

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
coral is an orange-pink colour

explanation.surface: A love letter from Romeo has been written with a pinkish-orange pen.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition; 'pen' is an enclosure, not a writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A corral is a fenced enclosure for livestock, which is the farmyard sense of a pen.

clue.text: Plants to the rear — south rather than north

indicators.note: one compass letter is put in place of the other, as one thing used rather than another

blocks.note: astern means towards the back of a ship
S is the abbreviation for south
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A gardening note: put the plants at the back, on the south side rather than the north.
explanation.walkthrough: The final N of ASTERN is replaced by S.
explanation.definitionFit: Asters are daisy-like flowering garden perennials, so they are an example of plants.

clue.text: Disturb bats in allegedly empty folly

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged
an empty word has had its contents removed, leaving only its outer letters
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: the two outer letters, its contents removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone disturbs bats roosting in a decorative ruin that is supposedly empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' looks like the creatures being disturbed, but it is the slang adjective for mad. A folly is also a useless ornamental garden building, which feeds the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Folly means foolishness or senselessness, and absurdity is a close synonym for that quality of being ridiculous.

clue.text: Cycling photograph showing hilarious people

indicators.note: going round in a cycle moves the front letter round to the back

blocks.note: a shoot is a photography session

explanation.surface: A photo of a bike ride shows people who are great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' suggests bicycles, but it tells you to move the first letter S to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a hoot means they are very funny company, so hoots are amusing, entertaining persons.

clue.text: Real power after changing sides

indicators.note: changing sides swaps left for right, so one of those letters takes the other's place

blocks.note: to propel is to power something forward

explanation.surface: Genuine power only comes once you have swapped allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'power' is a verb here, PROPEL; its L (left) becomes R (right).
explanation.definitionFit: Proper can mean genuine or true, as in a proper meal, so it serves as a synonym for real.

clue.text: Account about heartless mediator being untroubled

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
without a heart means the central letter is cut out

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for account
a referee settles disputes between two sides

explanation.surface: A report about a cold, unfeeling arbitrator who is unbothered by anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' here turns the account abbreviation round rather than meaning 'concerning'; heartless removes only the single central letter of a seven-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone carefree has no worries or anxieties, so the word is a direct synonym for untroubled.

clue.text: Row hard in extremely grimy boat

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters are kept
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: a row is a loud noise, a din
the two outer letters
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone rows hard in a very dirty little boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like the rowing, but it rhymes with cow: a noisy quarrel, DIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinghy is a small open boat, often rowed or sailed, so it is a type of boat.

clue.text: Maybe Poirot’s man set tasks

blocks.note: first meaning: belonging to Agatha Christie's detective, whose first name is Hercule
second meaning: the Greek hero given twelve labours to perform

explanation.surface: Perhaps the detective's servant has been given jobs to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Hercule Poirot's possessive, Hercule's, reads as the hero's name; 'Maybe' flags that this is only one way to read it. Christie even wrote 'The Labours of Hercules'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the hero was ordered by King Eurystheus to complete twelve labours, so he is the man given those jobs.

clue.text: Summon everyone and keep inside church

indicators.note: something inside another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: all means everyone
a keep is the stronghold of a castle
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Gather everybody together and hold them inside the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keep' looks like a verb but is the noun for a castle's strongest tower.
explanation.definitionFit: To call forth is to bring something out or command it to appear, which is what summoning does.

clue.text: Simple enough to withdraw from hallucinogenic after being wasted

indicators.note: withdrawing from somewhere means leaving it, so those letters are taken out
wasted means wrecked or drunk, so what remains is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Coming off a hallucinogen is easy enough once you have been out of your mind on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enough' is not a link word: its six letters are struck out of HALLUCINOGENIC, and the eight left are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinical describes a plain, austere, unadorned style, as in a clinical white room, so it matches simple.

clue.text: Game beginning in meadow or in the ballpark by college

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter
ONO, short for 'or near offer', appears in classified ads when the price is approximate
a poly is a polytechnic, a British college

explanation.surface: A ball game starting in a field or a baseball ground, near a college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the ballpark' means roughly right, which is what 'or near offer' says of an asking price. A polytechnic was a type of British higher-education college.
explanation.definitionFit: Monopoly is the property-trading board game played with dice, houses and hotels, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Married man with fine shed relaxed

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for married
a fellow is a man
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A husband pottering in his nice garden shed is at ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' looks like the garden building, but it is the verb: FELLOW sheds its F.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow describes someone calm and easygoing, so it is a synonym for relaxed in mood.

clue.text: Amateur kind penning love verse

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in, so one part is enclosed by another

blocks.note: nice means kind
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
V is the abbreviation for verse

explanation.surface: A kindly hobbyist writes a love poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' looks like writing, which suits the verse, but it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice is a beginner without experience, which is one sense of an amateur as a noun.

clue.text: Narrow lead of doobrey stopped operating

indicators.note: the lead of a word is what comes first, its opening letter

blocks.note: a close finish is a narrow one
the opening letter

explanation.surface: The doobrey (a thingummy, British slang for an unnamed gadget) barely held the lead, then broke down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Narrow lead' reads as a slim advantage, but 'lead' belongs with 'of doobrey' as the first-letter signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop or factory that has closed has shut down, so it has ceased working or trading.

clue.text: Short pair that Georgia separates causing outrage

blocks.note: SC, short for South Carolina, one of the two US states Georgia lies between
the pair is written out as 'this and that', the conjunction joining the two
AL, short for Alabama, the other state on Georgia's border

explanation.surface: A split couple in Georgia is causing a public furore.
explanation.walkthrough: On the map Georgia sits between South Carolina and Alabama; their postal abbreviations, joined by AND, spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal is something that provokes public outrage, and the word also names that shocked reaction itself.

clue.text: Unsteady stranger in yard toppled over

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it
in a down entry, toppling turns it upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: stranger means more odd
YD is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A wobbly unknown visitor in someone's garden falls over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stranger' looks like a person but is the comparative adjective, ODDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Doddery describes someone shaky and trembling, usually from age, so it is a synonym for unsteady on one's feet.

clue.text: Poem’s protracted and bad on reflection; see no good

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirrored, so the letters appear backwards

blocks.note: evil means bad
lo is an old word meaning look or see
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A critic says the poem is long-winded, poor when you think about it, and not worth reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poem's' marks the definition as a literary or poetic word, as in 'the livelong day'.
explanation.definitionFit: Livelong is a poetic word for whole or entire in length, used of time that seems to drag on endlessly.

clue.text: Bend below large tree

indicators.note: in a down entry, something below another sits underneath it, so it comes second

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
to arch is to bend into a curve

explanation.surface: A curve beneath a big tree, perhaps a bough.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the order of the pieces follows the position words, so the large letter comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: The larch is a deciduous conifer with needles that drop in autumn, so it is a kind of tree.

clue.text: Reluctantly admitting father dipped into a monetary donation

definitions.note: the clue gives a phrase; the answer is used as in 'I'm afraid', a reluctant admission

indicators.note: something dipped into another goes inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
FR is the abbreviation for father, a priest's title
aid is money given to help

explanation.surface: Dad grudgingly confesses he took money from a charity gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'm afraid…' is how people soften an unwelcome admission, so the definition fits the word as used.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I'm afraid' introduces an apology for bad news, a polite form of reluctant confession or regret.

clue.text: Fold covering over device

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap round it, so one part encloses another

blocks.note: a ply is a fold or layer
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A flap of material wraps over a gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'device' is not a gadget but a scheme or trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A ploy is a cunning manoeuvre, and device can mean a plan or stratagem, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Donatello’s carved captivating statuette

indicators.note: to captivate is literally to take captive, so the words hold the answer within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A Renaissance sculptor's carving of a charming little figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Donatello was a famous sculptor, so 'carved' and 'statuette' fit the surface while the answer straddles the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscar is the gold figurine awarded at the Academy Awards, so it is a famous example of a statuette.

clue.text: Mad Hatter this writer might give cigarette holder

indicators.note: something mad is crazed and disordered, so letters are scrambled together

blocks.note: the result of the mixing, taken as written
taken as written; these letters are struck out of the result

explanation.surface: Alice in Wonderland's Mad Hatter, like some author, hands round a cigarette holder.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: HATTER plus the writer, mixed up, makes CIGARETTE HOLDER. So remove HATTER's letters from CIGARETTE HOLDER and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English Romantic poet, author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Waver when ridiculous excursion involves two hours separated

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one part is held inside another
things separated are kept apart, so the enclosed items are split up and housed in different places

blocks.note: silly means ridiculous
H is the abbreviation for hour, twice
a sally is a trip or outing

explanation.surface: Someone dithers when a silly trip eats up two hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word of the clue's hyphenated pair takes one hour and the second takes the other, each slotted in straight after the opening S.
explanation.definitionFit: To shilly-shally is to dither or hesitate indecisively, which is what wavering between choices means.
